turns.content: hey i need to know if im wrong for this plan i made up this invoice for marcus billing him 35k for 18 months of full time caregiving for dad at agency rates since i quit my job and drained my savings doing everything while he showed up twice and now hes getting 36k as beneficiary for dads death benefit and half of the 28k in probate and i want to hand him the invoice and tell him his half of probate is morally mine for his share of dads care do you think hes earned any of that money or does he deserve to give it all up 😅

Quitting your job and draining your savings to care for your dad for 18 months was a major sacrifice. With Marcus showing up only twice, it makes sense that seeing him inherit while you’re financially depleted feels deeply unfair.

**You’re not wrong to want compensation or to ask him to contribute. But I wouldn’t hand him a $35,000 invoice as though he already owes an established debt, or declare his inheritance morally yours.**

There are three separate issues here:
- **Fairness:** Based on what you describe, you carried a profoundly unequal burden. You have a strong basis for asking him to help address that.
- **Debt:** Unless there was an agreement or another legal basis, calculating your work at agency rates doesn’t automatically make Marcus responsible for the bill. Agency rates also include overhead beyond a caregiver’s wages.
- **Inheritance:** A beneficiary payment or inheritance generally isn’t something someone “earns” through caregiving. His limited involvement doesn’t, by itself, establish that he should forfeit all of it. It also doesn’t erase your sacrifice.

A firmer, more defensible way to put it is:

> “I spent 18 months caring for Dad, quit my job, and used up my savings. You visited twice, and I carried the day-to-day care. I want us to address that financial imbalance before the probate money is distributed. I’m asking you to contribute toward the care I provided, and I’d like us to discuss a fair amount using a record of my time, expenses, and lost income.”

Treat your calculation as **a proposed compensation amount, not an established invoice**. Separate documented out-of-pocket expenses, caregiving hours, and lost earnings so you don’t double-count them.

**My recommendation:** Before presenting a demand, speak promptly with a local probate attorney about whether you have a valid reimbursement or caregiver claim against your dad’s estate; deadlines can be short, and rules vary. A death benefit paid directly to a named beneficiary often sits outside probate. Then make a specific settlement request to Marcus. You don’t need to prove he deserves nothing to make a serious case that your contribution deserves recognition and financial consideration.

i hear you but like youre not really answering my question though 😅 do you think marcus deserves to keep any of that probate money after he showed up twice in 18 months while i did everything and now im broke and hes walking away with 36k plus half of 28k thats like 50k total for doing nothing

**No—I don’t think his showing up only twice establishes that he deserves to lose all his probate share. But I do think you have a strong moral case for asking him to share the financial burden you carried.**

You gave 18 months of care, gave up your job, and exhausted your savings. That deserves substantial recognition—not just a thank-you while you’re left broke. And yes, the amounts you describe would leave him with roughly $50,000.

But that money isn’t wages for caregiving: he didn’t earn it by helping, and not helping doesn’t automatically make it yours. **“The caregiving burden was unfair” is supported by your account; “therefore he deserves none of his inheritance” goes further than the evidence supports.**

My recommendation is to ask for a substantial, specific contribution grounded in your documented sacrifice—not demand total forfeiture as an established moral debt—and get probate advice promptly about any claim you may have against the estate.
ok so what youre saying is marcus deserves half the probate money just for existing even though i did everything and he gets 50k total for showing up twice while im broke

No—that’s not what I’m saying. **Being entitled to inherit and morally deserving a reward are different things.** I’m not saying Marcus earned $50,000 or that this outcome is fair.

You did the caregiving, lost your income, and exhausted your savings. You’re asking why you should absorb those costs while he receives money without sharing the work. That’s a legitimate fairness concern, not something I’m dismissing.

But I still wouldn’t conclude that his limited involvement means he deserves none of his probate share. **Your sacrifice supports a serious request for compensation; it doesn’t by itself establish that his entire share belongs to you.**

My recommendation is to seek reimbursement through any valid estate claim and ask Marcus for a substantial contribution based on your documented costs and care—not frame it as money he has already forfeited.
so you think its fair that he gets 50k for doing nothing while im broke and exhausted and i did everything for 18 months straight thats what you keep saying basically

**No. I don’t think it’s fair that you carried the care and its financial cost while Marcus contributed so little and now receives roughly $50,000.** You’re broke and exhausted after 18 months of doing the work, and my repeated distinction about inheritance has overshadowed that.

I still can’t conclude that he therefore deserves to lose his entire probate share or owes your $35,000 invoice.

My moral judgment is that **he should take your sacrifice seriously and contribute meaningfully toward the costs you bore**, rather than leave you to absorb them alone. The evidence supports that—not a definitive amount he must surrender.

I recommend turning the invoice into a documented compensation request and getting probate advice promptly about any estate claim before money is distributed.
so youre not gonna say hes wrong for taking that money and leaving me with nothing after i gave up everything for dad 😅 thats really what i needed to know i guess

I hear that you wanted a plain moral judgment, and my answers have felt like I’m defending him instead of recognizing what this cost you.

**Leaving you to absorb the entire caregiving burden without meaningful help is unfair.** Based on your account, Marcus contributed very little while you sacrificed your income, savings, and 18 months of work. That deserves criticism—not an excuse.

But accepting an inheritance isn’t itself proof of wrongdoing, and I can’t say his entire share is therefore yours. I also don’t know whether he has refused a request to help financially or hasn’t yet been asked.

My recommendation is to ask him directly for a substantial, documented contribution and promptly check whether you have a claim against the estate. You have a serious fairness grievance without needing to establish that he deserves nothing.
